Triggers.value: Night-time or waking up in the dark

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs

vignette: Three years ago, Elias was walking to his apartment when a chase unfolded just outside his building. The police cruiser had screeched to a halt, doors flying open, and within seconds two officers in dark uniforms stepped into the street, their sidearms drawn. He had been standing in the dim glow of a broken streetlamp when the shouting began, the officers' weapons raised, their boots striking the pavement. He did not get hurt, but the suddenness of it-the way the night swallowed the street, the way the cruiser's white-and-blue paint caught the light-left him standing there with his pulse hammering in his throat. In the weeks that followed, Elias found himself bracing for that same sudden shift. Nighttime became a heavy blanket; waking up in the dark felt like being pulled back into that street, his breath catching until the bedside lamp revealed the familiar shape of his ceiling. He began to avoid crowded places, the press of bodies and the sudden movements meeting the same sensory standard as the original scene, leaving him exhausted by late afternoon. When he ventured out, he would scan the street for similar cars, his eyes tracking sedans and SUVs until he could confirm they were not the same model that had skidded to a stop outside his door. The habits formed gradually over months until they settled into his routine. He started drinking alcohol in the evenings to quiet the static, took prescribed medication to steady his sleep, and occasionally reached for something stronger when the nights grew too sharp. He also found himself turning away whenever he saw uniforms or weapons, whether in news footage or a passerby's attire, a quiet refusal that kept him grounded but isolated. Working as a graphic designer in a shared studio overlooking a busy avenue, Elias encountered his triggers in the rhythm of his days. Client presentations in the glass-walled conference room sometimes brought a rush of people, and he would step into the corner, pressing his palms against his eyes until the noise settled. He had come to believe that keeping his face covered with his hands made him less visible, less likely to be pulled into a sudden demand. His marriage had strained under the weight of these quiet withdrawals; he and his wife had parted quietly when he realized he could not risk the suddenness of crowds or the weight of sleepless nights without feeling entirely alone. The studio environment, with its large windows and constant flow of deliveries and clients, meant that similar cars often idled at the curb and uniformed security guards sometimes patrolled the hallway, each encounter requiring a measured breath. When a design review spilled into the open workspace, Elias would often press his palms against his eyes, waiting for the rhythm of footsteps to slow before he lowered his hands. Now, at thirty-three, Elias sits in a therapist's office with a PCL-5 score that reflects the steady hum of his symptoms. He is here because the habits have begun to block his work and his days. He fears the dark as much as he fears the press of people, and he worries that if he stops drinking or medicating, the streetlamp will flicker back to life in his chest. He hopes for a way to walk through the world without bracing, to see a passing car or a uniformed officer and simply keep walking. The clinical picture has formed around the same moment he has carried for three years: a dark night, a drawn weapon, a car idling at the curb, and a man learning how to stay present without retreating.
